 5 Expenses Your 2027 Social Security COLA Could Help Cover
 Jordan Rosenfeld 2026년 11월 14일 토 오후 11:30 UTC 0 Ridofranz · Getty Images Social Security recipients are getting a raise in 2027, but it won’t feel like a windfall. On Oct. 14, the Social Security Administration announced that the cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) would be 3.6%, adding roughly $75 a month to the average retirement benefit, though each person’s bump depends on their current check. 
 The annual COLA, is designed to help benefits keep pace with inflation, but it may not be enough to overhaul a retirement budget . The smart move is deciding in advance where the extra money goes, so it covers real expenses instead of quietly disappearing.
 Worth Noting: 3 Food Assistance Programs That Can Help Retirees Beyond SNAP 
 Keep in Mind: 8 Clever Ways Retirees Are Earning Up to $1K Per Month From Home 
 Here are five places the increase could do the most good.
 1. Healthcare
 For retirees who have Medicare Part B premiums deducted from their Social Security checks, any premium increase could eat into the COLA before it reaches the rest of the budget. In a 2026 KFF tracking poll , 49% of Medicare beneficiaries age 65 or older said they expected healthcare costs to become “less affordable” in the coming year.
 The extra money could cover higher Part B premiums, prescription copays, dental care, vision needs or hearing services. Those out-of-pocket costs add up quickly.
 Retirees with Medicare drug coverage can compare plans during open enrollment , which runs Oct. 15 through Dec. 7. If a different plan fits their prescriptions and budget better, they can switch.
 2. Groceries
 Groceries are a good place to direct a small monthly increase because food costs have increased significantly over the past couple of years. Food-at-home prices rose an average of 2.3% in 2025 compared with 2024, according to the USDA’s Economic Research Service (ERS). 
 More recently, the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) reported that grocery prices were up 1.8% in the 12 months through September 2026. Some categories saw larger increases in 2025: egg prices averaged 21.9% higher and beef and veal prices 11.6% higher.
 Advertisement
 Stretching the increase is easier than it sounds. A warehouse club can save money on bulk staples, and store brands at a regular grocery store often deliver similar quality for less. 
 3. Utilities
 The COLA announcement may be a welcome boon to anyone living in an area with seasonally high bills. Retirees expecting higher than usual utilities could transfer all or part of the monthly increase into a separate account for months when electricity, natural gas or water bills run higher.
 The money could also fund small fixes that lower future bills, like replacing an HVAC filter or adding weatherstripping where drafts sneak in. 
 4. Transportation and Gas
 Retirees may not commute anymore, but gas prices still find them. Gasoline rose 34.2% between September 2025 and September 2026, according to the BLS , and that hits even occasional drivers. 
 For retirees who still drive, the extra cash can cover fuel, oil changes, tires or a future repair. 
 5. An Emergency Buffer
 Anyone without an immediate need for the extra money could put it into emergency savings . A dedicated buffer can cover a home repair, an insurance deductible or another surprise without leaning on high-interest debt. 
 Saving the full $75 average increase each month would add up to $900 over a year, before any deductions. Actual amounts will vary based on each person’s benefit and Medicare premium deductions. 
 Personalized COLA notices will appear in the message center of a mySocialSecurity account starting in late November, but only for people who enroll in paperless notices by Nov. 18. 
 The Bottom Line
 The COLA won’t transform anyone’s retirement, but it can quietly solve a few real problems if it has a clear assignment. Pick the expense that worries you most, give it a dedicated slice of the increase, and set it up before the first higher check hits. Money with a job is far less likely to vanish into the usual monthly chaos.
